edges.effect_quant: In the coronary-heart-disease trial, an app-based reminder and education package improved medication nonadherence scores after 60 days, but pilot app trials in discharge and cardiovascular settings remained small and feasibility-focused, making the broader adherence effect real but inconsistent in strength.
edges.population: patients using smartphone apps to log, track, or support medication-taking habits
edges.mechanism: Habit-tracking apps make invisible routines visible by turning dose-taking into a recorded, reinforced behavior. They can improve adherence when reminders, check-ins, and feedback become part of a daily loop, but they rely on sustained user engagement, so the benefit weakens quickly if patients stop opening or trusting the app.
edges.summary: App-based adherence support looks promising, but the evidence is not uniformly strong enough to call it a settled win. Some randomized trials show better medication-taking and symptom outcomes when apps are used consistently, yet many studies are still pilot-sized, condition-specific, or vulnerable to declining engagement over time, so this edge is best treated as mixed rather than unequivocally protective.
edges.caveats: The intervention category is heterogeneous: some apps emphasize reminders, others self-monitoring, education, video check-ins, or social accountability. That makes it hard to separate the effect of habit tracking itself from the effect of the surrounding behavioral scaffolding and from the problem that more motivated patients are often the ones who keep using the app.
